t: Apply Operations to Maximize Frequency Score
o: With at most k ±1 increments, maximize the frequency of any value. Sort the array; making a contiguous window of sorted values all equal minimizes cost, achieved at the median. So the question becomes: the largest window whose median-alignment cost ≤ k. Costs are computed in O(1) with prefix sums. Example 1: sorted [1,2,4,6], window [1,2,4] aligned to 2 costs 1+0+2=3 ≤ k=3 → answer 3.
k: Optimal windows are contiguous in the sorted array, aligned to the median.
Window cost = Σ|nums[i] − median|, computable in O(1) with prefix sums.
Binary search the window length (feasibility is monotone) or use two pointers.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search on window length
a.i: If a window of length L is affordable, so is any smaller one; binary search L and test all windows of that length.
s: Sort nums, build prefix sums P
cost(i, j) via median m: nums[m]·(m−i) − (P[m]−P[i]) + (P[j+1]−P[m+1]) − nums[m]·(j−m)
Binary search largest L with some affordable window
a.t: O(n log² n) — binary search over lengths, each checked in O(n)

a.i: Since adding an element to a window never decreases its minimal alignment cost and removing never increases it, a two-pointer sweep finds the maximal affordable window in O(n) after sorting.
s: For each right end, shrink left while cost(l, r) > k
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting plus amortized O(n) two-pointer sweep

w: Use the two-pointer version for optimal complexity; binary search is easier to justify. k up to 10¹⁴ and sums up to ~10¹⁴ demand 64-bit integers (BigInt in JS). Pitfall: aligning to the mean instead of the median is wrong; also remember the target value need not exist in the array beforehand.
